title: Jerusalem falls (2 Kings 25)
hookLine: the temple burned, the people carried to Babylon
carry: even exile is not the end
last: THE BOOK WAS LOST IN THE HOUSE.

lines: THE SIEGE, THE FAMINE, THE BREACH.
cards: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." That psalm is sung by people a very long way from home. How did they get there?
The answer is in a hard chapter at the end of Second Kings. An army from Babylon surrounds Jerusalem. The siege goes on until there is no bread left in the city.
The wall is broken through. The king, Zedekiah, runs for it by night and is caught near Jericho. And then the Babylonian commander comes to the city with fire.

teach.h: THE HOUSE OF THE LORD BURNED.
teach.b: The King James Bible tells it flatly, almost like an inventory: "he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire."
The temple Solomon prayed in, gone. The walls pulled down, the bronze pillars broken up and carried off as scrap.
The rest of the city is carried away to Babylon, and the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and fields.

teach.h: CARRIED AWAY OUT OF THEIR LAND.
teach.b: "So Judah was carried away out of their land." That's exile: not just moving, but being taken from the place where your God's house stood, to a city where everything says your story is over. Here's what's worth noticing.
The burning is the obvious ending, but the chapter keeps going. Years later in Babylon, a new king lets the old exiled king of Judah, Jehoiachin, out of prison, and "he spake kindly to him."
New clothes instead of prison garments, and a seat at the king's table every day for the rest of his life.
That's the last scene of the whole book. Not a rescue, not a return home.

teach.h: A SEAT AT THE KING'S TABLE.
teach.b: Just a man in exile, eating at a table, spoken to kindly. Some readers hear a small sign that the line of David isn't finished. Others simply hear that the story kept going.
And the psalm from the opening is sung from inside that exile. A people who lost their land did not lose their voice.

how: Christians read the fall of Jerusalem and the exile in Bible readings and sermons, sometimes alongside Psalm 137 and the prophets, and some churches pray for refugees and displaced people when these passages come up.

o: a sentence served in a royal prison
being carried away from your own land
a long journey to a holy city to worship

it ends later in the chapter, with the exiled king Jehoiachin eating at the king's table in Babylon.
everyone in Judah was taken to Babylon

games.q: you're writing the history of your people, and you've just told how the temple burned and the people were carried away. how do you end the book?
o: with the fire. there's nothing left to say.
with a lament for everything lost.
with the exiled king spoken to kindly and given a seat at the table.
games.why: 2 Kings ends with Jehoiachin out of prison, in new clothes, eating at the king's table. not a return home, but not the end of the story.

practice: Bring to mind people who've lost their homeland: refugees in the news, a family that moved to your street, a coworker who can't go back, maybe your own grandparents.
Picture one face, or one family, at their kitchen table tonight, a long way from where they started, without trying to solve anything.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words, by name if you know it; if you don't, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Exile. Being carried away from your land, as Judah was taken to Babylon when Jerusalem fell and the temple burned.

orig.note: Hebrew: exile, being carried away from the land.
